title: GAAC: Lossless KV Compression for Bandwidth-Efficient LLM Inference on Personal Devices
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:GAAC: Lossless KV Compression for Bandwidth-Efficient LLM Inference on Personal Devices
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Weight-only, lossy quantization substantially reduces the storage and memory requirements for serving large language models (LLMs), but the growing key-value (KV) cache remains a bottleneck for long-context inference on personal devices. We present Group-Adaptive Additive Codec (GAAC), a lossless KV compression and serving system that exploits exponent redundancy to reduce storage and accelerate attention without introducing KV approximation. GAAC encodes BF16 exponents using calibrated per-channel base-plus-offset codes over contiguous ranges. GAAC adapts code widths across small groups while preserving KV values bit-for-bit. A fused attention kernel reconstructs KV tiles on the fly, avoiding full-cache decompression. Block-wise compression and fixed-capacity slots support incremental cache updates and paged serving. Across five tested models, GAAC achieves 1.405-1.407$\times$ lossless BF16 KV compression. We also study compression performance on low-precision tensors FP8 E4M3 caches ( 1.09-1.14$\times$) and E5M2 caches (1.25-1.30$\times$). On NVIDIA DGX Spark, GAAC accelerates decode attention at a 64K-token context by 1.19-1.27$\times$ and end-to-end W4A16 decode steps by 1.04-1.15$\times$. In serving, it reduces resident KV memory by approximately 26% and increases aggregate throughput by 13-29% under comparable KV-memory budgets. On Apple M4, GAAC achieves 1.02-1.25$\times$ attention speedups, demonstrating portability beyond NVIDIA GPUs.

report.summary: GAAC is a lossless KV-cache compression system that cuts memory and bandwidth for long-context LLM inference on personal devices.
report.background: Large language models are increasingly expected to run long-context inference on laptops, workstations, and other personal devices, where memory capacity and bandwidth are tight. Weight-only quantization has made model weights smaller, but the key-value (KV) cache—one set of keys and values per layer per token—grows linearly with context length and can dominate memory during serving. Existing KV-cache compression often uses lossy quantization or eviction, which can alter model outputs and complicate quality guarantees. GAAC instead exploits redundancy in BF16 exponent bits, aiming to shrink the cache without changing any KV value. The work fits a broader push toward bandwidth-efficient inference: faster attention kernels, paged serving, and hardware-aware codecs that make long prompts and multi-turn chat practical on consumer hardware rather than only in data centers.
key_points: GAAC targets the exponent fields in BF16 KV caches: instead of approximating values, it stores calibrated per-channel base-plus-offset codes over contiguous ranges and adapts code widths across small groups. The decoded KV values remain bit-for-bit identical, so long-context quality is not traded away for memory savings.

The system pairs compression with a fused attention kernel that reconstructs KV tiles on the fly, avoiding full-cache decompression. Block-wise compression and fixed-capacity slots allow incremental cache updates and paged serving, which matters for real serving workloads where new tokens arrive continuously and memory is allocated in pages.

Across five tested models, GAAC reports 1.405–1.407× lossless BF16 KV compression. Compression is smaller for low-precision caches: 1.09–1.14× for FP8 E4M3 and 1.25–1.30× for E5M2. That suggests the technique works best where BF16 exponent redundancy is largest, not as a universal multiplier.

On NVIDIA DGX Spark, GAAC speeds 64K-token decode attention by 1.19–1.27× and end-to-end W4A16 decode steps by 1.04–1.15×. In serving, it cuts resident KV memory by about 26% and raises aggregate throughput 13–29% at comparable KV-memory budgets. Apple M4 attention speedups of 1.02–1.25× show portability beyond NVIDIA GPUs.
report.impact: For the AI industry, GAAC is a reminder that inference efficiency is not only about weight quantization: KV-cache traffic is a first-order cost for long-context serving. A lossless codec could complement lossy weight quantization and paged attention, especially on memory-constrained devices. Developers may benefit if the approach is integrated into serving frameworks, but the modest 1.4× BF16 ratio means it is not a replacement for more aggressive lossy methods; kernel support and codec overhead will determine real gains. For regular users, the practical payoff is longer contexts, more concurrent sessions, or faster decode on personal hardware—if vendors adopt it. The Apple M4 results are encouraging, but broader model and hardware validation is still needed.
report.tools: Watch vLLM’s PagedAttention and KV-cache management, NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM, llama.cpp and MLC-LLM for on-device serving, Apple MLX for M4-class hardware, and Hugging Face Transformers’ cache utilities. Since GAAC is an arXiv paper, check for an official code release and whether it lands in these stacks; for experimentation, start with paged-serving frameworks that expose custom KV-cache layouts and fused attention kernels.
